Hi Alice — quick technical explainer to make the billing and caching behavior concrete. TL;DR: Redwood bills by tokens (input + output). Characters are an approximation; requests are just API calls. Caching can avoid billed model compute if the response is served from a server-side cache we control (see notes).

Details:
- Tokens vs characters: there is no fixed 1:1 mapping, but a practical rule of thumb is ~4 characters per token for English text (so 1,200 characters ≈ 300 tokens). This varies with punctuation, code, or non-Latin scripts.
- Billing unit: Redwood charges per-token (we sum input tokens + output tokens for a request). Example pricing math (illustrative):
  • If price = $15 / 1M tokens then:
    – 1M tokens -> $15
    – 10M tokens -> $150
    – 50M tokens -> $750
  • If your average request is 300 tokens in (prompt) + 200 tokens out (completion) = 500 tokens/request -> 1M tokens ≈ 2,000 requests.
- Requests vs tokens: requests are just an activity count. You can have many small requests (lots of network overhead) or fewer larger requests (more tokens per request). Billing is unaffected by request count — the cost driver is total tokens processed.
- Caching: Redwood supports multiple caching layers:
  1) Client / app-layer caching: if you cache request/response at the app and never call the API, you are not billed (because no call is made).
  2) Redwood server-side prefix/KV caching: when enabled, identical prompt prefixes can be served from cache without re-running the model; in that case we do not bill full model compute for the cached portion. How billing is applied depends on cache hit semantics:
     - If the entire response is returned from cache (cache hit), there is no model invocation and you are not billed tokens for that invocation.
     - If only a prefix is cached and we still run the model to compute the rest, we bill only for the tokens generated by the model run (plus any small metadata tokens we charge for bookkeeping).
  3) Note: app-layer caching that returns the exact response also results in zero billed tokens (because no Redwood call is made).

Quick worked example using your numbers:
- You reported ~1,200 chars/request -> ~300 tokens/request (input). Assume a 200-token completion average -> 500 tokens/request total.
- At 1,000,000 tokens: cost = $15 (using $15 / 1M as example).
- If you do 2M requests/month at 500 tokens each -> 1,000,000,000 tokens -> 1,000 * $15 = $15,000 (this is to illustrate scaling math; we'll tailor to your ranges).

Practical recommendations to control unit economics:
- Batching: combine small requests where possible to reduce per-request overhead and improve throughput.
- Prompt engineering: truncate/format prompts to reduce unnecessary tokens.
- Leverage prefix caching for highly repetitive system prompts/state. This can dramatically reduce model compute and billed tokens for repeated interactions.

I've attached a short CSV with example cost buckets (redwood_sample_costs.csv). Marissa — if you want, we can fill the spreadsheet with $/1M scenarios (e.g., $8, $12, $15) and our estimates for your 30M–80M range.
